source: Money debates people already argue about, each side stated as its own best case with the place that case is made. The app is the referee: it runs both sides on the person's numbers and names the flip point, the one figure where the answer changes. It never picks a side in general.
confidenceNote: The sides are summaries of public arguments, attributed to where they are made; the summaries are this file's, not quotations. Each debate's arithmetic is a named function in engines/debates.js, on shared engines, never a rule of its own.
note: Read by engines/debates.js (K3, D-218). `fn` is the engine function; `reads` are the Ledger fields the run needs; `flip` names the one figure the answer turns on.

debates.name: The Middle Class Trap
debates.question: Is a net worth that is mostly home equity and retirement accounts a trap before 59 and a half, or a planning problem?

sides.label: It is a trap
sides.case: A high net worth on paper, mostly the house and the 401(k), leaves too little money to live on before 59 and a half; the bridge years cannot be funded without penalties.
sides.source: BiggerPockets Money podcast, the 'middle class trap' episodes (Mindy Jensen and Scott Trench), 2024.

sides.label: It is solvable
sides.case: The Roth conversion ladder, 72(t) payments and the Rule of 55 reach retirement money early without the penalty, given lead time; the trap is a planning gap, not a wall.
sides.source: ChooseFI (Brad Barrett and Jonathan Mendonsa) with Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, 2024 episodes on the trap.

flip.label: years of bridge money
flip.note: the ladder needs the bridge to cover its seasoning years; with fewer, only 72(t) or the Rule of 55 reach the pre-tax money without the penalty

debates.name: Pay off the mortgage or invest
debates.question: Does an extra dollar go to the mortgage or the market?

sides.label: Pay it off
sides.case: A guaranteed return at the mortgage rate, no market risk, and a paid-for home changes how much you need to retire.
sides.source: Dave Ramsey, The Total Money Makeover (Baby Step 6); the case for a guaranteed return.

sides.label: Invest it
sides.case: Over long periods a diversified portfolio has returned more than a mortgage costs, and money in the market stays reachable; a low fixed rate is cheap money to keep.
sides.source: JL Collins, The Simple Path to Wealth; the expected-return case.

flip.label: the mortgage rate against the real return
flip.note: investing wins when the return beats the mortgage rate; the range says whether that holds across a poor decade and a good one

debates.name: Roth or traditional
debates.question: Pay the tax now, or later?

sides.label: Traditional
sides.case: Most people pay a lower rate in retirement than while working, so deferring the tax wins; the deduction now is worth more than the tax later.
sides.source: The Finance Buff (Harry Sit), 'The case against Roth 401(k)', and the marginal-rate framing in Bogleheads' wiki.

sides.label: Roth
sides.case: Tax paid now at a known rate buys freedom from unknown future rates and required distributions, and a Roth dollar is a whole dollar.
sides.source: Ed Slott, The New Retirement Savings Time Bomb; the rate-risk case.

flip.label: your marginal rate now against the rate at withdrawal
flip.note: traditional wins when the rate now is higher than the rate your spending would be taxed at later

debates.name: 4% or lower
debates.question: Is 4% a safe withdrawal rate, or should the number be built on less?

sides.label: 4% holds
sides.case: Thirty-year retirements at 4% of the starting pot survived every historical period the Trinity study tested; a lower rate means working years longer for safety that history did not demand.
sides.source: Cooley, Hubbard and Walz, 'Retirement Savings: Choosing a Withdrawal Rate That Is Sustainable' (the Trinity study), 1998, and Bill Bengen's 1994 paper.

sides.label: Lower for long retirements
sides.case: Fifty-year retirements at today's valuations fail often enough at 4% that 3.25% to 3.5% is the safe figure; the extra years of saving buy the difference between fine and ruin.
sides.source: Karsten Jeske (Early Retirement Now), the Safe Withdrawal Rate Series, part 1 onward.

flip.label: the withdrawal rate
flip.note: the two numbers and the years between them; the flip is the rate the pot you will have supports

debates.name: One more year
debates.question: Does one more year of work buy safety, or just cost a year?

sides.label: One more year
sides.case: A last year of saving and growth adds a cushion for the whole retirement, and the sequence risk of the first years is the one that sinks plans.
sides.source: Wade Pfau on sequence-of-returns risk; the cushion case.

sides.label: Go now
sides.case: One more year becomes another; the pot supports the spending already, and a year of life is the price nobody puts on the spreadsheet.
sides.source: Mr. Money Mustache, 'The 4% rule: the easy answer to how much do I need for retirement', and the one-more-year syndrome writing at Can I Retire Yet (Darrow Kirkpatrick).

flip.label: what the pot supports against what you spend
flip.note: go now when the pot already supports the spending; one more year when it does not, and this says by how much it would

debates.name: Rent or buy
debates.question: At these prices and this rent, which is the better use of the money?

sides.label: Buy
sides.case: A fixed payment that ends, equity instead of rent receipts, and a place nobody can raise the rent on.
sides.source: The case for owning as consumer guides state it; Zillow and Census price-to-rent framing.

sides.label: Rent
sides.case: When the price is high against the rent, the difference invested beats the equity; renting keeps you mobile and out of the costs of owning.
sides.source: Ramit Sethi, I Will Teach You to Be Rich, on renting; the price-to-rent rule of thumb in consumer guides.

flip.label: the price-to-rent ratio
flip.note: buying favoured under the lower band, renting above the upper, neutral between

debates.name: Pay off low-rate student loans or invest
debates.question: Does the extra go to the loan or the market?

sides.label: Pay them off
sides.case: A guaranteed return at the loan rate, no market risk, and a debt gone for good.
sides.source: Dave Ramsey, Baby Step 2; the debt-free case.

sides.label: Invest
sides.case: A low fixed rate is cheap; the expected return on a diversified portfolio is higher, and federal loans carry protections a brokerage account does not need.
sides.source: The Money Guy Show, the Financial Order of Operations on low-interest debt; the expected-return case.

flip.label: the loan rate against the real return
flip.note: investing wins when the return beats the loan rate; the range says whether that holds across a poor decade and a good one
